Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition, utilizing a heavy reliance on real-time scenes supplemented by brief, subtle moments of exposition to fit its slice-of-life style. 

Because the narrative spans only about twenty minutes—covering a single morning crossing of a cable ferry—it unfolds almost entirely as a continuous, real-time scene. The story relies on immediate sensory details (the fog, the cold metal, the dripping water), physical actions, and sparse dialogue to create a quiet, grounded atmosphere. 

Extended summaries would disrupt the slow, observant pace of the crossing. Instead, the writer weaves in micro-expositions naturally within the scene: Ilse recognizing the crack in the van's headlight and knowing the driver knows where to park (showing they are regulars), or noticing that the boy's face on his monthly pass photo is still round (showing the passage of time). This restraint makes the final moment—when Jonas calls and she chooses not to answer—all the more intriguing and impactful, as the lack of explicit backstory leaves the emotional weight entirely in the subtext of her actions.
